prize_parts.citation: For the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles, in which pKa-tuned charge switching and lipid self-assembly encapsulate and deliver nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Having read the full first round, I keep ionizable lipid nanoparticles as my single-part preference. The chemical content is a design principle: a lipid whose pKa is tuned so it is near neutral in blood and cationic in the acidic endosome, combined with controlled self-assembly and lipid phase behaviour, solves the problem of packaging a large polyanion and releasing it in the cytosol. It is the only one of the three leading candidates with approved medicines at global scale (patisiran and the mRNA vaccines), so demonstrated consequence is not promissory. It also transfers to gene-editing delivery, protein replacement and other nanomedicine, which is the test I apply: did it change what chemists and clinicians can actually do. The chair's question about the 2023 Medicine prize is answered by the citation itself, which honours the vehicle and the pKa and phase-behaviour chemistry, not the nucleoside-modified payload. I keep Anderson as the third name because the combinatorial lipid lineage is what produced the potent lipids used clinically, alongside the Vancouver design work of Cullis and Hope.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakest point. Madden, MacLachlan and Langer are left out, and the Vancouver and Boston lineages overlap, so any three-name cut is contestable. The 2023 Medicine prize still covers adjacent territory, and a reader could treat this as a second recognition of the same advance unless the citation stays strictly on delivery chemistry. Finally, a single-part prize leaves the chemistry of modalities such as degraders and base editing unrecognised this year.

responses.point: Linke proposes a two-part prize pairing base editing (Liu) with ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Hope), and argues the pair is coherent around making nucleic acids programmable and deliverable.
responses.response: I welcome his support for the lipid part and I can accept Cullis and Hope as a minimum, but I would not move to his pairing. Both parts would be nucleic-acid medicine, adjacent to the 2020 CRISPR and 2023 Medicine prizes, which is exactly the risk he names himself. He also concedes that degraders may be the cleaner pure-chemistry second part. His Liu-alone base-editing seat also drops Komor and Gaudelli, who did decisive experiments, so I see the pairing as raising the attribution problem rather than solving it. If the committee wants two parts I would rather pair B052 with B042, though I would still prefer one part.

responses.point: Aqvist keeps targeted protein degradation first as a simple chemical idea that opened the undruggable proteome, with a coherent story from the PROTAC concept to cereblon.
responses.response: I agree it is a strong chemical idea and I keep it as my first alternative. The chair's maturity question matters to me, though. No PROTAC drug is approved, and he himself notes the glue strand sits awkwardly with the 2001 PROTAC paper, so Crews, Deshaies and Handa are arguably two achievements under one citation. Ionizable lipids have a settled mechanism and approved products used by hundreds of millions of people, and the lipid citation has fewer lineage conflicts than a PROTAC-plus-glue citation. If degradation prevails I would want the citation explicit about which strand it honours.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first as a defined chemical reaction, deamination without double-strand breaks, and says his preference would give way to a more clearly chemical modality if it is judged medicine or biotechnology.
responses.response: His own caveat is close to my view. The adenine editor, with TadA evolved to act on DNA, is genuinely chemical, and I rank base editing as my second alternative. But it dates from 2016 and 2017, long-term safety and off-target deamination are not settled, and Target-AID makes the attribution unresolved among Liu, Komor, Gaudelli, Nishida and Kondo. Since he is open to yielding if the chemistry-versus-medicine framing goes against base editing, lipid nanoparticles are a mature alternative with a clean chemical citation.

responses.point: Sparr prefers biomolecular phase separation but ranks lipid nanoparticles second, framing them as lipid self-assembly and colloid chemistry.
responses.response: Her lipid self-assembly framing is the one I want in the citation, and I accept her disclosed adjacency. On phase separation, my doubts about generality and the Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag credit split remain, so I would not support it this year. If her round-1 preference cannot reach five votes, I hope she can accept B052, since it rests on the physical chemistry she values.

uncertainties: Whether Madden, MacLachlan or Langer should displace Anderson or Hope, or whether the Vancouver and Boston lineages can be fairly divided at all under three names
Whether a citation strictly on delivery chemistry keeps the prize clear of the 2023 Medicine recognition of nucleoside-modified mRNA
Whether the committee will accept a nucleic-acid-adjacent prize (B052 alone) or prefers one that includes a pure small-molecule modality such as B042
Whether expert reports will settle the PROTAC and glue question enough to make B042 the more widely acceptable choice
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requires recusal. I have a research-field overlap with Emma Sparr in self-assembly and peptide-lipid systems and a translational interest in nanomedicine, but no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Cullis, Hope, Anderson or any other shortlisted candidate. Nothing in the first round changes this disclosure.
